title: Meeting a neighbour
setting: You're renting a room for a month in a quiet kampung, a neighbourhood of narrow lanes, in Yogyakarta. As you head out one morning, the older woman next door is sweeping her front yard.

n1.speaker: neighbour
n1.english: Morning! Where are you off to?

options.feedback: The stock vague answer. Mau ke mana? is a greeting, so nobody expects details.
Greet her back, then a two-word answer: that's all she's after.
It sounds as if you're asking why she wants to know. Mau ke mana? is a friendly greeting, like 'how's it going?', so answer it lightly: Jalan-jalan saja.
No 'am' needed: dari (from) does the work.

options.indonesian: Dari Selandia Baru, Bu. Dari Auckland.
options.feedback: Adding your city gives her something to ask about next.
There's no 'am' in Indonesian, and adalah, the formal written 'is', never goes before dari. Saya dari Selandia Baru.

n3.speaker: neighbour
n3.indonesian: Wah, jauh sekali! Bahasa Indonesianya sudah bagus, ya.
n3.english: Wow, that's a long way! Your Indonesian's good already.

options.feedback: Modest and hopeful: the natural way to take a compliment on your Indonesian.
Telling people you're learning wins you patience, and usually more praise.

options.indonesian: Ya, bahasa Indonesia saya bagus sekali.
options.english: Yes, my Indonesian is very good.
options.feedback: Agreeing with a compliment sounds boastful. Wave it off modestly: Saya baru bisa sedikit.

n4.speaker: neighbour
n4.english: How long are you here for?

options.english: Until the end of the month.
options.feedback: Sampai kapan? is literally 'until when?', so sampai plus a time answers it.
Lagi after a length of time makes it 'more': tiga minggu lagi, three more weeks.
Sampai jumpa is goodbye. She asked Sampai kapan? (until when?), so answer with a time: Sampai akhir bulan.

options.indonesian: Sudah, Bu, terima kasih. Ibu sudah makan?
options.feedback: Sudah is the yes to a Sudah …? question, and asking back with Ibu in place of 'you' is warm and polite.
A Sudah …? question is answered sudah (yes, already) or belum (not yet). Tidak sounds as if you don't eat at all.
Kamu is for friends, children and people younger than you. To an older neighbour, say Ibu instead: Ibu sudah makan?
Mari, Bu is the polite goodbye as you walk on.
A gentle, polite way to take your leave. Dulu (first) softens it.
Selamat jalan is said to someone setting off on a journey. You're the one leaving, so say Mari, Bu.

end.speaker: narration
end.english: A typical morning chat. Mau ke mana? and Sudah makan? are greetings that show friendly interest, and Jalan-jalan saja or Sudah, terima kasih answers them perfectly. Use Ibu or Bapak, not kamu, with older neighbours, and wave off compliments on your Indonesian modestly.
